title: Las Casas
hookLine: a Spanish colonist priest in the Americas turns against conquest and defends indigenous people

cards: A priest sits down to prepare a sermon. He's also a landholder on a Caribbean island, with indigenous Taíno people forced to work his land.

He opens the book of Sirach, sometimes called Ecclesiasticus, one of the books Catholic and Orthodox Christians count in the Old Testament, and reads about offerings made from what was taken unjustly.
The bread of the needy, it says, is their life, and whoever takes it from them sheds blood. He stops. He can't preach on it and keep living as he lives.
So he does what his neighbors won't. He gives his laborers up.

teach.b: Bartolomé de las Casas came to the Americas as a Spanish settler, in the wave that followed Columbus.
Under the system the Spanish called the encomienda, settlers were granted indigenous people to work for them, in theory to be protected and taught the faith, in practice often worked without mercy.
Las Casas took part, and was even ordained a priest while still holding his grant. Before his turn, Dominican friars in the islands had spoken up.
One of them, Antonio de Montesinos, preached to the colonists asking, in effect: are these not human beings? Do they not have souls? Are you not bound to love them as yourselves?
The colonists were furious. Las Casas knew that challenge, and later came his reading of Sirach.

He gave up his grant, years later joined the Dominicans, and spent the rest of his life arguing, in pamphlets, in books and before the Spanish court, that the native peoples were free human beings, and that conquest and forced labor were sins.

He wrote a searing account of the destruction of the Indies, and debated a scholar who defended the conquest. Our line gathers up what he argued: they are our brothers. Jesus says it in Matthew: "all ye are brethren."
There's a hard part, and it belongs in the story.
Early on, Las Casas suggested bringing enslaved Africans to spare the native people. Later he wrote that he regretted it, and that enslaving Africans was just as unjust.
Even a defender of the oppressed had to unlearn something. His story is honored by Catholics and studied far beyond the church.

how: Las Casas is remembered by Catholics, and especially by Dominicans and by Christians working for justice in Latin America, as a defender of indigenous peoples; his writings are still read in debates about conquest and human rights.

games.q: you're a priest and a landholder, preparing a sermon. the passage says whoever takes the bread of the needy sheds blood. what do you do?
o: preach it, and keep your land and laborers.
give up your laborers and start speaking out.
games.why: Las Casas gave up his grant, later joined the Dominicans, and spent his life arguing that conquest and forced labor were sins.

practice: Bring to mind someone whose work you rely on and rarely see: the person who picked your food, sewed your clothes, cleaned the building. Hold them as a brother or sister, with a face and name you don't know.
If you pray, pray for them; if you don't, simply hold them in mind.
